label: Length Spaces
notes: This chapter, printed pages 32 through 46, builds distance out of curves. We promise three things: a length functional on paths, a length metric defined by infimum, and the Hopf-Rinow payoff that completeness plus local compactness force geodesics to exist and closed balls to be compact.

label: Length of a Curve
notes: We define the length of a path as the supremum over partitions of summed consecutive distances. Stress that this uses only the ambient metric, not smoothness. A curve is rectifiable when this supremum is finite, and length is additive under concatenation and invariant under reparametrization.

label: The Induced Length Metric
notes: Here is the central construction: the length metric assigns to two points the infimum of lengths of paths joining them. Emphasize that this infimum may be larger than the ambient distance, may be infinite if no rectifiable path exists, and always dominates the original metric.

label: Chord versus Path
notes: Walk through the sphere picture carefully. The ambient chord cuts straight through space, while the intrinsic distance must stay on the surface. The gap between them is exactly what the length metric measures, and it is why intrinsic geometry differs from the geometry of the surrounding space.

label: Length Spaces
notes: A length space is one where the metric already equals its own induced length metric, so distance is realized arbitrarily well by joining paths. Contrast this with the chord metric on the sphere, which is not a length metric until we replace it by arc length.

label: Mid-points and Approximate Geodesics
notes: In a length space distance is approached by paths but geodesics need not exist. Introduce approximate mid-points: points almost equidistant whose distances to the endpoints nearly sum to the whole. Completeness will later upgrade these approximate mid-points into genuine mid-points and then into geodesics.

label: Completeness and Local Compactness
notes: State the two standing hypotheses precisely. Complete means Cauchy sequences converge; locally compact means every point has a compact neighborhood. Neither alone suffices, but together, in a length space, they are exactly the conditions Hopf-Rinow needs to deliver properness and geodesics.

label: Proper Metric Spaces
notes: Define proper: every closed bounded set, equivalently every closed ball, is compact. Properness is strictly stronger than completeness. The Heine-Borel property gives us convergent subsequences for free, which is the engine that extracts limit geodesics from sequences of approximating paths.

label: The Hopf-Rinow Theorem
notes: State the theorem cleanly. For a length space that is complete and locally compact: it is proper, hence closed balls are compact, and it is a geodesic space, so any two points are joined by a length-minimizing geodesic. This is the chapter's keystone result.

label: Proof Architecture
notes: Sketch the logic without full detail. Local compactness propagates outward so that the radius of compact balls is open and closed, hence all of the space; that gives properness. Properness plus completeness lets approximate mid-points converge to mid-points, and iterating builds the geodesic.

label: Why the Hypotheses Bite
notes: Show the necessity with counterexamples. The open disc is locally compact but incomplete, so a diameter has no geodesic. An infinite-dimensional sphere is complete but not locally compact, and closed balls fail to be compact. Both hypotheses are genuinely required.

label: Synthesis
notes: Recap the pipeline: curves give length, length gives an intrinsic metric, and the length-space condition makes that metric self-consistent. Completeness and local compactness then convert intrinsic distance into honest geodesics. This is the bridge from metric spaces to the geodesic spaces of the next chapter.
